Lessons.Title: Name Parts as Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Which One Doesn't Belong four source rectangles have exact labels grounded in HTML: A blue L-shaped region with half the total AREA although the outline is irregular; B rectangle divided into3 equal vertical parts with one part shaded1/3; C rectangle split by off-center line into UNEQUAL regions, not halves; D rectangle with top half shaded1/2. A,B,D each show equal area partitions, C does not.

Activity1 Partition the Strips requires a SET OF SIX originally equal-size paper strips per pupil. Reserve one representing whole1, and fold one for each unit fraction1/2,1/4,1/8,1/3,1/6. Draw pencil marks at original vertical folds and label EVERY individual piece. Fourths can come from halving halves, sixths from halving thirds, and eighths from halving fourths. KEEP the physical fraction strips for subsequent lessons.

Activity2 Partition, Shade, Trade first asks to partition five rectangles into halves, thirds, fourths, sixths and eighths then label all parts correctly. Next, students independently partition a blank rectangle into some number of EQUAL parts and shade EXACTLY ONE, without labeling or showing partner. They trade shapes and each identifies the other pupil's unit fraction and explains the numerator1/denominator relationship.

Synthesis visually contrasts an original six-equal-part rectangle labelled1/6 in EACH region with a six-part rectangle showing ONLY ONE shaded1/6; 'sixths' names kind of equal parts, 'one sixth' names the single shaded region. Original illustrations inspected, publisher SVG path artwork not embedded.

The public teacher lesson requires MLR8 partner conversation and actual fold/mark/trade evaluation. Original blackline Strip master/pupil PDF and protected Label the Parts Cool-down were not separately read; no Stage D, tests or academic approval.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal-sized parts
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fractional part requires equal area, even if shape outlines differ.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original A L-shaped colored region is a half.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: One of n equal areas in a whole.
KeyConcepts.Example: One shaded among six equal regions is1/6.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction strip
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal-sized wholes partitioned into differently sized unit parts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Reserve one whole; label all individual pieces.

KeyConcepts.Title: Shade and Trade
KeyConcepts.Definition: Pupil-generated unlabeled unit fraction is inferred by a partner.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count equal parts, confirm exactly one shaded.

WorkedExamples.Title: Warm-up A
WorkedExamples.Question: Can an L-shaped shaded region be half of rectangle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal parts of a whole and shade only one as specified.
Steps: Count equal area of the irregular blue region versus white.
Even with different outline, the two areas match.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original A yes, original C no.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original thirds
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangle has3 equal regions, one shaded.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal parts of a whole and shade only one as specified.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fold sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Use six equal areas.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal parts of a whole and shade only one as specified.

WorkedExamples.Title: Partner trade
WorkedExamples.Question: Pupil shades one of eight equal regions, without label.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal parts of a whole and shade only one as specified.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Each of6 parts is1/6 but one is shaded.
WorkedExamples.Method: Count equal parts of a whole and shade only one as specified.
Steps: One highlighted part is ONE sixth.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reject original A half because colored area is L-shaped.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A's differently shaped blue and white regions have equal AREA.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Call original C halves because it has two pieces.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source off-center divider gives unequal pieces.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confuse six strips with six different denominators.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source provides six total equal-sized strips: one for whole and five for fractions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Automatically grade a prescribed n in the exchange activity.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Pupils choose their own partition and hide the fractional label.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher/partner check any n allowed and one shaded.

SummaryPoints: Original warmup A and D half,B third,C unequal; A can be L-shaped.
Create original six-strip collection; fold five strips into2,3,4,6,8 parts.
Secret partition-shade-trade partner explanation is intentionally nonunique.
Each equal part1/n; only one is shaded in original synthesis example.
